It addresses the problem where geometrically calibrated cameras still produce inconsistent pixel values for the same radiance due to sensor differences or lighting variations [S2].

The claim states that geometrically calibrated cameras produce inconsistent pixel values for the same radiance due to sensor differences or lighting variations. Source [S2] Section 7.1 explicitly states: 'Although we have geometrically calibrated the cameras... we have not color calibrated them... We need to ensure that one radiance value will be converted to the same pixel value for each of the cameras.' It further explains that the system introduces gain and bias to 'account for slight differences in overall intensity in the image.' This directly supports the claim that despite geometric calibration, intensity/radiance-to-pixel conversion is inconsistent and requires correction.

Optimizes geometric parameters, such as detector orientation and source position, during reconstruction to correct for calibration errors [S1].

The claim states that the system optimizes geometric parameters (specifically detector orientation and source position) during reconstruction to correct for calibration errors. Source [S1] explicitly states in the 'Geometric Self-Calibration' section: 'our system can optimize the geometric parameters, such as detector orientation and source position, during the reconstruction.' It further explains that this process allows the pipeline to 'recover from this bad initial calibration' (where bad initial calibration was simulated by adding noise to position and rotation), thereby correcting for these errors.

It is chosen when initial camera poses are inaccurate or noisy [S1].

The claim states that the method is chosen when initial camera poses are inaccurate or noisy. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly mentions adding 'Gaussian noise to the position and rotation of each view to simulate bad initial calibration' and demonstrates that the system (GSC) 'recovers from this bad initial calibration'. Since position and rotation of views correspond to camera poses, the evidence supports the claim.

Unlike [Color Volume Optimization and Density Initialization](842-color-volume-optimization-and-density-initialization.md) which adjusts volume properties, this method adjusts the observation model [S2].

The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly describes a method that adjusts the observation model. Specifically, Section 7.1 details the introduction of 'per-camera and per-channel gain and bias' applied to the reconstructed image to account for intensity differences. Section 7.2 provides the equation for the final image pixel, which includes these gain and bias parameters applied to the volume color before merging with the background. This confirms that the method adjusts the observation model (via gain, bias, and background estimation) rather than adjusting volume properties directly in the manner described for the contrasting method.
supported

Estimates a static per-camera background image $I_{\text{rgb}}^{(\text{bg})}$ to capture stationary objects outside the reconstruction volume, reducing artifacts caused by slight appearance differences from calibration errors or view-dependent effects [S2].

The claim states that a static per-camera background image is estimated to capture stationary objects outside the reconstruction volume, reducing artifacts from calibration errors or view-dependent effects. Source [S2] explicitly confirms this in Section 7.2, stating that the background image is 'static across the entire sequence, capturing only stationary objects that are generally outside of the reconstruction volume.' Furthermore, Section 7.3 explains that artifacts caused by 'calibration errors or view-dependent effects' are reduced by the system's ability to compensate, and Section 7.2 notes that 'This background estimation process greatly reduces the amount of artifacts in the reconstruction.' Thus, all facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported

Radiometric Self-Calibration optimizes per-camera and per-channel radiometric parameters (gain and bias) during the reconstruction process to correct for photometric errors and intensity mismatches between cameras [S1, S2].

The claim states that Radiometric Self-Calibration optimizes per-camera and per-channel radiometric parameters (gain and bias) during the reconstruction process to correct for photometric errors and intensity mismatches. Source [S1] explicitly mentions 'Radiometric Self-Calibration' and notes that it involves 'exposure and sensor bias estimation' during reconstruction to correct for 'photometric errors'. Source [S2] explicitly defines 'Color Calibration' (a form of radiometric calibration) as introducing 'per-camera and per-channel gain and bias' applied to the reconstructed image to account for 'intensity differences' (intensity mismatches) and mentions that reconstruction priors help compensate for 'calibration errors' (photometric errors). Both sources confirm that these parameters are optimized/estimated within the reconstruction pipeline.

It is chosen when the scene contains static background elements that the volume reconstruction might otherwise try to model incorrectly, leading to smoke-like artifacts [S2].

The claim states that the background estimation (implied by 'It') is chosen when the scene contains static background elements to prevent the volume reconstruction from modeling them incorrectly, which leads to smoke-like artifacts. Source [S2] Section 7.2 explicitly states: 'In our training data we often have static backgrounds that the algorithm will try to reconstruct... To ensure that our algorithm only reconstructs the object of interest, we estimate a per-camera background image'. Furthermore, Section 7.3 states: 'Without using priors, the reconstructed volumes tend to include smoke-like artifacts... The system can learn to compensate for these differences... To reduce these artifacts...'. The notes also confirm that estimating the static background image reduces artifacts caused by calibration errors or view-dependent effects. Thus, the evidence fully supports the claim.
